[h1][i]Beneath [b]DUSK.[/b][/i][/h1]
The message Dusk delivers is, "Hey, have you ever wanted to play Quake or Doom, except that it takes place in Silent Hill? Don't worry, neither has literally anyone else, but you're welcome!"

[h1] "Things have gone wrong. Very wrong. Better kill everything." [/h1]

DUSK is a first-person shooter (FPS) developed by David Szymanski and published by the company New Blood Interactive. They are also responsible for the publication of AMID EVIL.  

[i] Pros & cons: [/i]

++ Hop. Hop. Hop. You will be strafe hopping at breakneck speed, while doing back flips, and shotgun the nearest redneck cultist in the face. Speed and skill-based gameplay are the stars of this show. Simply addictive. 

+ Awesome soundtrack by music mastermind Andrew Hulshult. His contribution is essential for the successful immersion into this grim and delightfully evil world. 

+ Do you like dodging projectiles filled with life-defying energies? Highest difficulty level is too easy? Good, then Duskmare is your first choice! Anything that touches you, be it the nibbling of a rat or stubbing your pinky toe, will instantly kill you.

- Unfortunately, the protagonist lacks characterization. He is basically a bearded, silent Indiana Jones, dressed as Caleb from Blood (1997). My '90s nostalgia demands some memorable one-liners, or badass cutscenes.

[i] Summary: [/i]

DUSK stands tall among the other giants of the FPS genre; not as an imitation, but as an evolution. And I embrace it, with all its glory and all its horror.

Recommended for treasure hunters and old-school FPS gamers, who hallucinate the floor is lava.

[i] Achievements: [/i]

Estimated time for 100% completion: +15 hours

Singleplayer achievements: 29
Multiplayer achievements: 1

Dusk is a 1st person shooter inspired by the likes of Quake both in visual style and level design. It takes place in a fictitious town of Dusk, Pennsylvania.  It is fast paced with non-regenerating health and a bevy of weapons ranging from dual wielding shotguns, double barrel shotgun, dual wielding pistols, scythes', a mortor, rifle, and an exploding rivet gun.. among others.

The game is excellent for those who remember both Doom and Quake's frantic twitchy finger play style. Homage to the 90's FPS is evident throughout. Dusk uses the Unity engine and is one of the best examples of what that engine can do.

Graphics are low res by design, yet.. very exotic and colorful at times. They match the Lovecraft like atmosphere very well.

Sound and music are there but are also low fidelity, again an homage to the 90's shooters.

I really like the game. There are three episodes, each containing multiple missions, to go through. There is also a multiplayer PvP mode for up to 16 players.

I highly recommend this game to all those who like old school FPS!

This is a game where you rotate your gun, rather than reload it.
This is a game where taking cover means picking up that barrel and taking it with you, rather than cowering like a sissy behind it.
This is a game where "getting stoned" means picking up boulders and throwing them at enemies until they explode into chunky meat-salsa.
This is a game where the graphics intentionally look like everyone and everything has sharp edges that you can cut yourself on.
This is a game without a sprint function, as you move at "9-year-old-on-a-sugar-rush" speed all the time.
This is a game where it's clear the developers had a real hard-on for old-school '90s FPS games like Quake, Doom and Blood, and this game exists as a love-letter to them all.

This is DUSK.

Fresh off of Doom 2016, I was craving another fast-paced shooter. Dusk? What's Dusk? When did this come out? 1995? Wait.... 2018? And they want 20 bucks for this? You must be joking. Wait.... the reviews are.... good???

By far the best 20 dollars I've spent on a game. No exaggeration. I was hooked for a week and took my time completing the game because I didn't want the experience to end. Dusk is the self-aware embodiment of everything that made 90's shooters legendary. If this game had been released during that area - we would be mentioning Dusk within the same breath as Half Life and, Quake and Doom. Without a doubt.

[h1]200 character summary[/h1]
Dusk is an amazing fast paced horror FPS in the style of the classics. It has great level design with keys and weapons that feel just right, The sound is stellar, Also has Online and workshop support.

[h1]Story & Characters [b]7/10[/b][/h1]
There is a story, and it is pretty interesting with a nice ending, But it is played out with text in the beginning, Which is a real bummer, I loved what they did with Ion Fury. Surely you play and go trough some scenery, hear some voices and you can kinda make up what is going on, But the story did not really catch me sadly. But I am glad to confirm that the gameplay more than makes up for it.

[h1]Gamemodes & Gameplay [b]10/10[/b][/h1]
The game has a few gamemodes, You can play the campaigns, There are 3 episodes, and each episode has 11 levels, 10 normal ones and a secret level then you have a great endless mode where you can just kill waves of demons on 3 different maps one from each of the episodes. Then the game has a online mode, where you can kill eachother in an arena with 16 players max.

The gameplay is extremely fast paced, You move with high speeds and so do the enemies, There is no fall damage and you can even do flips mid air. There are jumppads which set you flying high. There are also powerups which enables you to climb walls, make you fire faster or Time only move when you move like in SUPERHOT. In DUSK you will kill demons with speed and style.

There is some great level design, The levels are pretty big, with the exception for boss levels. Most levels have a lot of keys which force you to explore a bit, There is not a lot of searching, unless you go for all secrets, The levels are packed with enemies, You will be shooting a lot in this game, But the game also gives you time to explore and enjoy the atmosphere

It really feels like a classic, the graphics, All the hidden mechanics are there. The keys, enemies. You can pick up almost everything and jump further by using explosives. It is like a FPS heaven with a lot of references to the classics. There are 10 great weapons to collect which all are pretty unique and have their place and ideal circumstances.

[h1]Graphics & Soundtrack [b]10/10[/b][/h1]
Yes it looks like a 90s FPS, But that's the style. there is a lot of detail in the textures and the levels are huge and look amazing. The soundtrack is just perfect, It is a Metal soundtrack, very nicely done. It is almost quiet at spooky moments which really enhances the horror elements, but it goes all out as soon as you are in a gunfight. Here the Metal kicks in and switches to a no time for fear atmosphere.

[h1]Performance & Support [b]7/10[/b][/h1]
The game has a few small things like Powerup sounds continue if you are in the pauze menu. It has these minor graphical glitches in the loading screens and the level select screen, But none of them ingame. Duskworld does not support controllers and if you try to launch it from Dusk it fails, You can manually start Duskworld from Steam tho. Other than that the game runs very smoothly I got between 90 and 150 fps on ultra. I read that the game will go open source, So I think it is based on GPL code? So even if the dev won't fix it before then, the community will. I have good faith these minor issues will be fixed.

[h1]Endgame & Replayability [b]9/10[/b][/h1]
The game does well in replayability, Especially for a FPS with a story mode. Ofcourse it has the online multiplayer which offers endless fun, Endless is a nice extra if you just like to shoot and kill. And the campaign has level select with a lot of secondary objectives which you can strive to complete. The game already has Mod support, And Steam Workshop is coming soon, So the game potentionally has endless content.

[h1]Improvements[/h1]
Surely the small issues need to get fixed, And ofcourse I would love to see more episodes, Other than that there are some things that could improve. Endless is a very nice extra, I just feel it could be more, Make us able to spend our score for keys to unlock areas with stronger weapons or who knows, The score attack mode is nice, But I think it could be more enjoyable if you took a little bit from the COD zombies games. We are also missing Online gamemodes. There is just Deathmatch, And nothing else, What happened to Teams, CTF, etc.

[h1]Workshop[/h1]
The game does not have workshop support yet. It will come soonish, The game has mod support already tho, You can already play many classics with the DUSK engine, Classics like Half Life and Quake are fully remade inside of DUSK. If you like modding DUSK is surely a game to add to your wishlist.

[h1]Conclusion [b]9/10[/b][/h1]
DUSK is like a mix between all the classics from the 90s, it took the best parts of them all, what made them unique and mashed it all together into 1 massive game. It is a must have for any classic FPS fan, Even people who don't like the graphics should just squint their eyes for one of the best FPS games of this decennia. It is an absolute must have.

This is a thumbs up, but with a caveat. The game itself is everything that's great about old school shooters. It's fun, fast, and straightforward. Its challange lies in quick reflexes and picking the correct weapon for the situation. The maps are varied and play well with the pixelated aesthetic. The developer clearly grew up on these games and understands their appeal well.

However.... For me personally, the game causes a great deal of eye strain. I'm not entirely sure what it is. I'm not someone who is sensitive to flickering lights, or other screen related issues. I played all the old school games this game takes inspiration from, and I have over 300 games in my Steam account, all of which I played without any problems. But this game wreaks murder on my eyes.

I think it's mostly caused by the way it handles lighting. The game has very aggressive muzzle flash, and you experience it in maps that are usually on the dark side. What lighting the maps do have, is dim and makes you strain your eyes to focus on the details. Add to it the fact that this game is really fast, and you get yourself a situation in which eyes that are straining in the dark to compensate for fast movement and dim lighting get attacked with strong flashes.

It seems that most people don't have a problem with this game, so I still thumb it up, but with a warning.

I really wanted to love this game, and first impressions were very good. I loved the speed, the crouch slide, the bunnyhopping, and it was interesting to see the game take on a much faster, looser speed than the classics it's based off. Unfortunately, despite my best attempts to really enjoy it, there are problems that add up to make it feel like a bit of a chore.

One such issue the level design; maybe it's unfair to compare this to ye olde Quake maps but with that game there are a lot of custom maps that put the vast majority of other games (and even id's own levels) to shame. I can't say the same for most of the levels in Dusk, since they generally seem to take place in either incredibly cramped spaces or far too open ones. Episode three has some cool, interesting scenarios in mid-sized spaces where you have to make use of the environment to outmanouver the enemies but these are few and far between, and almost non-existant in the first two episodes.

They also don't really have a lot of visual 'landmarks' to make them particularly memorible, and I got tired of seeing what is otherwise a boring-looking door be locked, knowing I'd have to backtrack when I pressed the incredibly small button to open it. Not that the triggers were difficult to find or anything, just that it doesn't really 'flow' as well as Quake did with it's huge, flashing touch-activated buttons and decorated doors to make navigation far easier and smoother - an absolute necessity when your game is built around speed. As it stands Dusk just feels very cluttered and same-y to look at and can get a bit tiring to play since the lack of landmarks take away a lot from the pacing when you have no real indication of how far into a level you are, making it all feel like a bit of a blur.

Placement of ammo, health and armour pickups are also not as important here than they ever were in Doom or Quake, with all of them being very sparse with enemies that drop ammo/health to make up the difference. This is not fundamentally a bad thing, Doom '16 managed to pull it off pretty well (even if I'll always prefer deliberate pickup placement to fine-tune how a given gameplay scenario will play out), but generally I found myself not really wanting to explore the levels outside of the admittedly cool secrets and easter eggs. I can think of only a handful of scenarios (most of them towards the end) where I actually wanted or needed to frantically rush around the level and search for ammo. The low maximum ammo count for many of the stronger weapons seems to encourage this but more often than not you'll just sequentially go through each one until the battle is over and you can run around to pick up whatever the enemies dropped. Quake had a pretty good solution to this problem by making every weapon uniquely useful (save for the non-super nailgun) but also having many of them share the same ammo pool, making it more of a choice to switch them based on the gameplay scenario rather than just 'I'm out of ammo, looks like I have to switch', which the lack of pickups seem to force you to do a lot.

Another minor issue with the weapons is that you're allowed to freely switch to completely empty ones. Not an issue by itself, but the HUD gives you no way to actually see the ammo pool for unequipped weapons, meaning you'll usually just be wasting time going through each one until you find one that actually has some ammo left. This breaks the flow and, again, can be detrimental to the experience in a game about speed.

Enemies are a huge problem, most of them seem to have poor telegraphing and extremely high projectile speed. One of these on their own is fine, but in tandem with the other it can feel more like a test of reflexes than an interesting gameplay scenario. Combined with the aforementioned cramped level design that leaves you with very little room to dodge them (and the fact that being even a few meters near them makes dodging impossible without bunnyhopping anyway), it can wear you down quite quickly. Especially when the game is more than happy to stick you in a room with large amounts of these guys, making it feel like a bit of a crapshoot as to whether you'll be able to dodge it all or not. On normal difficulty the perceived 'forced' damage taken from these instances isn't a huge deal but then you have no challenge, and on hard it can take off nearly half your health so every little hit means an awful lot. The worst offender for the telegraphing problem is the (for lack of a better name) dog-in-a-box enemy in episode 3, who can literally turn to face you from any angle and charge instantaneously; at least the lost souls from Doom had the courtesy to wait for a second before charging you. This problem is not limited to the dog and crops up with pretty much every other enemy type to a degree.

Some projectile enemies (like the big gun fella and the mini-boss lady) also track you through walls after leaving their line of sight. This wouldn't be as big of a problem (but arguably still not good design, IMO) if they didn't stop firing when you do this so there is zero indication that it's actually safe to go back into the fray, so you instantly get a face-full of damage if you attempt to come back out even a second before they've 'stood down' from this mode.

Enemy design seems to be lacking as well, namely the scientist dudes wearing nothing but lab coats who take two shotgun blasts to take down, yet the armored soldier enemies take just one. This isn't necessarily bad gameplay design but in Quake and Doom the enemies were generally representative of their HP bars, what with the bigger, louder enemies generally taking more to put down than the smaller ones. Another different example is the large cultists who shoot the homing fireballs, who feel like a missed opportunity for a new enemy design rather than just a larger version of the others, right down to their projectile sprite. An example of this done properly are the big and small knight enemies in Quake, who actually have different designs to complement the different strategies required to deal with them, despite both being dudes in armour when you boil it down.

This isn't to say this is even a bad game, and there are great things about it too. The soundtrack KFA. The weapons all feel sufficiently satisfying, though the mortar feels kind of useless and you only really bother with it when the rivet gun is empty. The sword made for some varied gameplay and I liked how it's reliance health/armour incentivised a different approach to dealing with enemies than the usual bunnyhopping-circlestrafing tactic. The atmosphere is pretty good, and the setpieces are excellent - really glad to see the game take full advantage of being on a more capable engine than Doom/Quake. It was cool to see the bounce pads from Quake 3 get ported over as they add even more dimension to the combat. Episode three is also quite a bit better in it's level design and visuals than the rest of the game, but it still feels flawed and the improvement isn't really enough to swing my overall opinion.

I don't want to discourage anyone who worked on this game. It's apparent everyone had a strong love for the old-school FPS greats. Soul just oozes out of every corner and underneath all of the problems there is a fantastic experience that has the potential to compete with the FPS legends. I genuinely feel they're onto something here and that's especially apparent in the third episode. Giving every aspect some fine-tuning and refinements could make this a GOTY conteder. I would love more than anything for them to give it another crack with a sequel, but as it stands I can't see myself going back to Dusk, unlike the games that influence it. However, this is a fantastic first attempt, and I'm looking forward to the next one - they may just be onto a winner.

There are some high highs and low lows in this package. The fast, frenetic shooting and steep difficulty is exhilarating and blisteringly fun. However, until you've played through certain maps multiple times, you'll be trapped in many a long stretch of running in circles looking for a wall switch or playing 'spot the difference' trying to find the one obtuse polygon of level geometry that moved when you were killing a mob of enemies on the far side of the map. Some people like this puzzling non-linear level design, but I sure don't. I frequently find myself grumbling at the game, telling it to hurry the fuck up and get back to the fun part.

I've beaten the game once on Medium difficulty by now, and have started chipping away on hard mode. When I have some time to kill and want to relax, I'll rerun missions on Game Journalist mode too. Rebinding the crouch slide / dodge roll command to my mouse-3 button changed my opinion of the game from a 6/10 to a solid 8/10. Slip&sliding underneath hadoukens and blowing a klansman's nose with a sawn-off-shotgun is an unparalleled delight. I just wish I didn't spend 3/4 of my time wandering aimlessly waiting for the fun part to kick in again.

I'm grumbling a lot, but I do recommend this game. Even among a genre that is bloated and flooded with repetitive and derivative experiences, Dusk is still very special, and has a lot to offer that no other game brings to the table. It's well-worth the price of admission, because I guarantee you'll like it more than I do.

Often when you see a game touted for being old-school, what that kind of praise really means is that the game in question is needlessly archaic, chained to the past and mired in empty nostalgia. I had been interested in Dusk since its reveal and was sort of worried that despite the aesthetic and design, once I jumped into the shoes of Duskdude, I would be disappointed at a game unwilling to look forward.

Thankfully, that is far from the case. As soon as you start up Dusk you realize that this isn't a game that is selling itself purely on you being able to remember Quake and Doom. This is its own thing, and it pays homage in small ways that add to, rather than distract from, the overall package. 

The level design is the standout feature for me, and what I'm going to be primarily focused on here. You start the game in a small house in rural Pennsylvania, having freed yourself from meathooks. Your only weapon is a pair of sickles, and without warning you are attacked by cultists brandishing chainsaws. Your surroundings are dank dungeon walls, and it's imperative you learn to circle strafe quickly to kill these maniacs without dying yourself. They have the advantage of numbers and weaponry, but you? You can move like you've been speedrunning 199X FPS games for thirty years. You will instantly feel just how precisely tuned the momentum of the game is, and soon you will learn how bunnyhopping isn't just an advanced component but a necessary part of every fight (though, graciously, Dusk puts more weight on you learning how to be efficient rather than precise timing, as bunnyhopping is simple and easy to learn). You also have the ability to pick up objects scattered around the areas, throwing them as weapons, making much of the environment more than just window dressing.

The level transitions from dungeons into a small house with cramped stairways and tight corners, something more in common with Rainbow Six than Doom. Once you get out of the house, you're treated to some fresh air and new enemy types as the game opens up into a small outdoor area. You're taught how to slide, adding another quick evasive maneuver to your arsenal, and then it's over. 

At this point, I'll admit to having been impressed but not overwhelmed. The game felt good, the enemies seemed fresh, the layout was cool. In the back of my mind, though, I was beginning to worry that the level design might be overly simple, that Dusk might be content with just setting up a couple boxes of spooky enemies per mission to shoot your way out of and calling it a day.
The mission after the first goes bigger and wider, opening up the outside areas and showing just how good these developers are at crafting buildings that are fun and tense to play through. I was wrong to have been worried, checking each new door and corner with apprehension and excitement. Powerups, dual-wielding, the game was broadening at a fast pace. A hedge maze area, filled with dread-inducing corners and dead ends, populated by shotgunning scarecrows. 

By the third mission, a level centering around a huge and horrifying church, I was completely hooked, but it was the ninth, penultimate mission of the first episode that made me a Dusk evangelist. Simply titled Ghost Town, this level sets you loose on a city block full of buildings to enter and explore, searching each nook and cranny for necessary keycards and bonus loot. Cultists on rooftops throwing fireballs from far away, soldiers with assault rifles lurking inside buildings. This level shows off just how good the game is at mixing claustrophobic close-quarters combat with long-range, hit-and-run battles. 

It's here that I'll stop talking about the levels, because in Episodes 2 and 3 of Dusk, the game throws new and unique concepts at you over and over, and each one deserves the surprise that the developers carefully craft. Instead, as my word limit draws near  and my time runs out, I'll do a quick rundown of everything else I liked and didn't.

The music is sublime, ranging from atmospheric tracks to fill you with dread to bass-heavy, pulse-pounding metal, making you ready to put an end to any cultists who dare to shuffle their masked selves towards you and your super shotgun.

The graphics, while intentionally rudimentary, still manage to look good and instill fear, and the use of color to break up drab palettes means you're never awash in a wave of samey areas. 

The guns are absolutely incredible, each one useful in different ways and each one a pleasure to learn the intricacies of. The shotguns are my favorite, but I really enjoyed the long-range hunting rifle for picking off troublesome enemy types from a relatively safe distance.

The bosses, which I was surprised to see exist, are each fun and provide interesting challenges (though some of them are also skippable if you so choose). 

That's about all I have to say about Dusk, a game I was enthralled with and finished in two sittings on the day I bought it. It is a fantastic game whether you're nostalgic for classic FPS games or not, whether you like horror or sci-fi, and regardless of how you feel about the super shotgun (though if you don't care for it, you are on the wrong side of history). I truly believe this to be one of the best shooter campaigns in the last few years and I'll be thinking about some of these levels (Escher Labs!) for years to come.

[h1] Introduction [/h1]
DUSK is an indie boomer shooter, made by David Szymanski, and I just want to say, I am GOBSMACKED at how good this game really is, especially given that majority of the development was a one man job.

[h1] Positives [/h1]
[list]
    [*]The story - You play as a treasure hunter, a person who learns about a sealed off town in Pennsylvania that is rumored to have hidden riches. He gets captured by the inhabitants and has to fight his way out, learning about what happened to the town and destroying the evil that's beneath it. Suffice to say, it was cool to see all kinds of demons and creatures, each being an "experiment" or "ritual" of sort. There's a guy that talks in your head throughout the entire journey, taunting, spiting and putting you to the absolute test and there's a good amount of things you can learn just from the places you go to

    [*]LEVEL DESIGN IS PEAK! I can't stress how good this is (at least for me personally) to be able to play a boomer shooter and not be stuck for at least 10 minutes. May just be a skill issue on my end, but shooters with backtracking and needing to remember things can be annoying, especially if or when the levels look the same or are hard to navigate, and I had little to no issues finding my way through each level of the game, even finding secret paths along the way! It's clean, easy to navigate and every level feels [b] different,[/b] even if there are ones that connect to one another in terms of looks, such as the facilities. David doesn't hesitate to change it up too, like having a level that lets you flip the entire world in order to get across or spawning in a massive tornado in order to get into a tomb. Easily the [b] best [/b] thing DUSK does

    [*]I really love the whole "Lovecraftian" gothic-ish sort of theme DUSK goes for here. It's different, unique and unlike any other boomer shooter I've played before, especially when we're talking horror (the only other I've played being DOOM 3, but that's debatable). It can be downright scary at times, especially with the way these things communicate to you

    [*]Pixelated graphics help to make DUSK feel like an old-school shooter from the 90's, which was clearly the intent. All kinds of references and inspirations, like Half-Life, DOOM, Heretic and Hexen to name a few. My favourite inspiration here would have to be the "Time Stim" or slow time power-up you can pick up. Straight from SUPERHOT in the way that time comes to a pause when you stop moving and resumes when you keep moving. Always nice to have modern game inspirations in something like this

    [*]Gameplay? Also peak. You start with these cool looking sickles before obtaining all of the weapons overtime. Guns feel crisp and strong, hit registration and feedback is solid and as far as I know, there's no sort of bloom, so just point and click! Great weapon variety, resources don't feel too scarce and each weapon has its own uses, so you most definitely won't just be using the one weapon the entire way through. Dual-wielding? No problem. Rocket launcher? This game's got it.

    [*]Enemy variety is THERE! So many different enemies, so much... time? Yeah, this game has heaps of foes to fight, from chainsaw dudes to military soldiers, scarecrows, cultists, flying things that look like D20 dice and many more. It's excellent, and I never found myself getting bored at all

    [*]SECRETS! I love these games for their secrets, and even though I'm not really good at finding them, it always felt rewarding and satisfying whenever I found one! I just got done replaying it for the second time and I managed to find a secret level I didn't find the first time in the first episode. I believe there's a secret level in every episode too. Most of the time it's just items, but sometimes you can find weapons that you normally don't get till later on, giving you an advantage. That alone should give you the reason to find these puppies

    [*]Boss battles are great, have good mechanics that encourage the player to lock in and dodge what they can and I didn't have any issues fighting any of them

    [*]Difficulties are well balanced - I played on the game's third difficulty and it felt just right, with good balance and no BS deaths, all of my deaths accumulating to how I played, not the game

    [*]Spinning your guns! If you press the reload button, you'll spin your weapon, which is great for style points and just spamming it whenever you're moving about the levels

    [*]Endless and Multiplayer modes - I can't speak for the multiplayer, but for endless, the mode is great and does exactly what you want it to do - spawn in one of 3 areas, start with just a pistol and survive for as long as you can, racking up a score and killing many demons. Great additions to the game and also includes difficulty settings for those who want to test their skills

    [*]Steam Workshop is a huge plus, adding replayability and giving you more ways to play DUSK. Some guy managed to make the entire first DOOM mission (the OG) into DUSK and it played so good!

    [*]The episodic approach is EXACTLY what I'd expect from this sort of game. Every episode puts you in a different part of the town and you hard reset your inventory whenever you enter a new one, as all things should be

    [*]Soundtrack is... well, it's freaking awesome. No words, just incredible stuff that really reminded me of modern DOOM
[/list]

[h1] Negatives [/h1]
There isn't really a lot I have to say in terms of [b] real [/b] negatives, instead I have a few nitpicks:
[list]
    [*]At some points in the game, the game has you implement a code sequence to open doors, which involves pressing two correct buttons in order to open it. It seems kind of silly to have it in a game like this, even though it's always used before or after a fight. I'm surprised that it stayed all this time after the release, but it's not too big of an issue if you play long enough to where the combinations become child's play, but to me, it's "why does this even exist?"

    [*]Bosses being "easy" to kill. I say it this way because I would always save my riveter/rocket launcher for bosses, never using it on anything else unless I needed to use it. Now I should note that I probably made it easier for a fight or two since I found it way before you're supposed to, but I still think I shouldn't be able to kill a boss with the 25 rocket capacity you can get. [b] Again, this is a nitpick,[/b] and the end of the day, I consider it to be a strategy more than anything else
[/list]

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Despite the nitpicks I have, I really don't have anything bad to say about DUSK. It's a incredible boomer shooter, with a Lovecraftian theme, excellent use of horror and some of the best gameplay and level design in this genre, ESPECIALLY considering that this is an indie game. The length of the game is solid too, it took me 5-6 hours for my first playthrough and I didn't suffer any performance issues. David Szymanski, thank you for creating this masterpiece. I highly advise all shooter fans to buy this game and play it. You'll thank me later.

I am prepared to make the bold and irresponsible claim that DUSK is so good that it's actually better than the id software classics it is trying (and succeeding) to imitate. And I love Doom to death.

It checks all the boxes: fast movement speed, lack of fall damage, intertwined and interesting maps (which are designed to be played with no starting weapons), plenty of secrets to find (none of which are timed, I think, unlike the ones in Doom!), and plenty of enemies to shoot with a variety of familiar weapons. On top of that, there are environmental objects that you can use in clever ways, though moving and manipulating them can be janky. And the game also plays with darkness in some levels, which I thought added to the atmosphere.

My only gripe with it is the music: it's good, but the intense battle action music kept playing when I had already killed all the enemies and was just exploring the map. It happened too often and got pretty annoying, so I had to disable it entirely.

I recommend playing on the second highest difficulty, Cero Miedo. The game will try to tell you that it's "not recommended for a first playthrough" -- ignore it, you'll be perfectly fine if you've played a video game before, and might even find it to be on the easy side. I do not recommend playing on the Duskmare difficulty, where you die from just one hit. Playing on Duskmare is tedious, especially if you're not savescumming, and requires you to become intimately familiar with the maps. That might not sound too bad, but you'll be forced to skip some of the sections and boss fights, and that's just not fun. Whichever difficulty you choose, absolutely do enable "intruder mode" -- that way, all the secrets you find will be much more rewarding and exciting.

Bonus fact: this game came out on same day/month that the original Doom did!

I'm late to the boomer shooter revolution, but I now see why Dusk is considered foundational in the genre.  The short answer: the level design is brilliant.  After playing through all three episodes, if I were to make a ranking of the most memorable FPS levels, Dusk would easily have several entries in the top ten.  The experience is varied from claustrophobic corridors to combat arenas to wide open spaces.  The environmental storytelling is top notch.  As the game progresses, the aesthetics of the environments change significantly and in interesting ways.  Just superb.

Secondly, and this is more a matter of taste, but I adore the horror-pastiche-as-theme vibe that Dusk exudes.    I caught references to Texas Chainsaw Massacre, The Witch and H.P. Lovecraft.  I'm sure there are many more references which went over my head.

However, it's not all sunshine and roses -- er, I mean, bloodstains and meathooks.

The weapons are... fine.  Pistols, shotgun, super shotgun, assault rifle.  You've seen all these before.  There are no secondary fire modes beyond 'look down scope'.  The most interesting weapons here are the shoot-through-walls crossbow and the sword which can charge and parry.  The most fun weapon is the mortar launcher, whose rounds can be detonated mid-air with a secondary click. 

The boss fights are merely perfunctory.  You'll not find more here than a fat health bar and a mess of bullets to dodge.  See 'Turbo Overkill' for a more recent entry which managed to do more to make boss fights interesting within the genre.

The final two levels of the game have a difficulty spike which seems a bit rough.  A late difficulty spike is certainly not unheard of for shooters, and you can adjust the difficulty setting at any time, so not a big deal, but it did put a slight blemish on an otherwise flawless level progression for me.

Still, despite my criticisms, I absolutely recommend a playthrough.  Dusk is worth it.

Distilling the best traits of old school shooters like Blood, Quake, Redneck Rampage and a few other titles of the past, Dusk successfully manages to pull everything off perfectly. While retaining the very essence of old school shooters it feels fresh and relevant in this age.

- The simple 3D graphics nail the nostalgic feeling of the early days and manage to set a cohesive tone to everything. The art style sets a perfect dark and gloomy atmospheric tone.

- Movement is fast, responsive and fluid and very similar to Quake 1 which amplifies the fast paced shooting mechanics of the game.

- You have various weapons at your disposal, they all feel powerful and the sound feels very satisfying.

- Enemies are varied and aggressive, each enemy is distinct and unique and some of them are downright creepy and stuff of nightmares. The AI is good does a good job at trying to kill you, this game gets difficult at the later stages, i would strongly recommend playing this on Hard difficulty.

- Level design is damn good, Dusk is divided into 3 episodes and each one feels unique. It is this very level design that keeps the game from getting repetitive and dragging.

- The sound design is amazing, especially the music. Andrew Hulshult has done the music for Dusk and he is the next Mick Gordon.

- Lastly I am a 31 yo grown ass man with other responsibilities and priorities in life, my attention span in gaming has drastically reduced over the years and i avoid average and mediocre games and yet I could manage to play and beat the game in 3 sittings which definitely means that this is a really good game.

Not really a game I can recommend to people in good faith. The developers of this game clearly put a lot of love and passion into this game based on the announcements and support, but I just couldn't get into it. It's a real shame, as I really [b]wanted[/b] to like this game, and I went in with hopes due to it being an overwhelmingly positive game, but all I got was a game I think is pretty boring. Apologies if I sound rude or uncaring in this review, as that's not the intent.

The biggest issue in this game can be summarized in just 3 words: [b]Lack of Variety.[/b]

For starters, enemies can be boiled down into 3 types. 
1) An enemy that runs at you and tries to melee you. 
2) An enemy that walks at you and tries to shoot you.
3) An enemy that runs at you and tries to either melee or shoot you depending on your distance from them.

3 is reserved for boss enemies, usually. Not that it matters, as you're still pretty fast compared to every enemy, and enemies that shoot at you won't attempt to track your movement with their shots at all. As such, the pretty universal strat for dealing with enemies in this game is circlestrafing around them holding M1 until they die. The game literally starts on an encounter with you being given only a melee weapon and just having to circlestrafe around 3 dudes with a chainsaw, holding M1 until they die. It gets old pretty quickly. 

With enemies in this game, your strategy or approach will rarely change, and outside of a very few enemy types, typically minibosses that become normal enemies, there isn't a huge need to prioritize one target over the other. To further my point, at the start of the game, there's a Scarecrow-type enemy that shoots at you with a shotgun, and the pellets/bullets from it spray out in a slow-moving RNG pattern. It can be avoided by simply pressing ctrl standing still, or walking in a straight like adjacent to him. However, later in the game, a new enemy is introduced, the skinny dudes with gaping narrow mouths. They basically do the same thing, they approach you and shoot a shotgun-like bullet pattern, but they're just faster, both in movement speed and projectile speed. It feels like the same enemy, just a new coat of paint.

I could only manage to get maybe towards the laterhalf of Chapter 3 without just saying "I'd love to play through this game fully to just see if it gets any better, but I've already gave it a fairer shot than most people who left a positive review." Regardless, I can say every boss battle up to that point is really just as much of a chore as regular enemies, beaten the same exact way, which is either running around in a circle holding M1 or just using splash damage from explosions around a corner. There is one boss that can be cheesed super easily by just standing on a staircase. I'm serious when I say just standing still on a staircase, even with no cover, just completely breaks the boss's AI and it doesn't know what to do, running around in a circle while you hold M1 and wait for it to die. Most enemies in this game don't know how to deal with stairs, but then again, most enemies in lots of smaller budget games don't know how either.

The lack of variety extends to even weapons, too. I don't know how this game did it, but it made me feel like there's no real difference between using pump shotguns, dual pistols and assault rifles. They all feel pretty similar. There's two sniper guns in the game, a Hunting Rifle and a Crossbow, and the only difference between the two is the Crossbow pierces, which I never really used outside of moments they clearly want you to use it, and remind you it can pierce. The explosive weapons have the most variety, but their ammo is the most scarce usually, on top of them both being incredibly powerful. There's about 10 total weapons in the game, give or take a bit as I might be forgetting some as they just don't stand out too much to me, and about 6 of them feel kinda just like the same thing. 

The level design is also kind of just a little annoying at times, and while it has the most variety to it out of most things in the game, I can't say I enjoy it. Once you get out of the first chapter especially, most of the combat encounters are typically started by enemies just kind of... appearing in the room you're in. The walls might just fall over and enemies spawn, you might press a button which causes enemies to spawn, sometimes they'll just appear out of nowhere. It got annoying, with me just sighing once I press a button I need to press to progress the level and then 30 enemies appear and I can't leave the area until I kill them. Visually, I wouldn't say the game is all that charming, and the level designs themselves can sometimes feel like a chore to traverse and search around. To touch on it as well, I wouldn't say the music is bad, but I mostly just don't notice it at all while playing. 

Then you have the fact the player character is pretty tanky on top of most enemies basically just being a bulletsponge. I'm not a big fan of games that do this, as it ends up just slowing down the pace of the game a lot, and I have to assume by this game giving you such fast movement speed on top of a (pretty useless) slide feature, they want the game to be fast. It just really isn't all that fast of a game, despite the desire for it to be. There's a lot more to fast-paced gameplay than simply moving fast and shooting fast.

And then you have just the aesthetic, stylization, "plot" and visuals. I put plot in quotations mostly just to talk about what the game is; You going around killing a bunch of Satanic KKK cultist dudes and spawns from Hell. As you traverse through the game, you go deeper into Hell and... kill more things, I guess. It's nothing unique, is what I'm getting at, and at this point it isn't really a charming aspect of the game. It needs more, and as I've established, it doesn't have too much going on with it. 

I've also got to say the horror aspect in this game is very lackluster. I can't tell if it's being played as a cheesy type of horror or trying to be played straight, but regardless it isn't a scary game whatsoever. The horror and jumpscares have only ever managed to annoy me, and don't even get me to slightly jump in my seat. Somewhere in CH2, the game introduces a Wendigo-like enemy. They're invisible and attack you, until you shoot them while they're invisible to reveal them. Once revealed, a horror zinger plays. This happens for every single Wendigo. Again, the horror in this game is just a mild annoyance at best.

So, to summarize, DUSK is a game that really doesn't have a lot to it. It's a game where you run around in a circle around enemies, holding the shoot button until they die, walking into the next room, and repeating the process. It's a very repetitive, tedious and lackluster gameplay experience that also lacks the general charm a lot of other games of this genre have, or their much more intricate gameplay elements. 

And here's the thing, if you enjoy games where you can just turn you brain off and run around holding M1 and gun down hellspawn and that makes you feel badass? Go for it. You'll probably love this game. But if you're like me and want something that's more engaging and mechanically interesting, you'd best look elsewhere. There's many other Retro FPS inspired by old games that do this while being far more mechanically deep and diverse than this game out there.

Much to my delight, there's been an influx of retro-FPS inspired games in recent years. I approached Dusk with a fair bit of cautious optimism, having been exposed to a bare minimum of gameplay. I've been down this road before; a game comes along, offering up a trip down nostalgia lane, a 100% accurate oldschool experience, only to fail on the delivery.

I went into this thinking Dusk would be okay, but only a mere imitation. Boy was I wrong. Let's break this game down.

Gameplay: This is the part where the game immediately sets itself apart from any imitators, and very early on establishes itself as a title to be taken seriously.. The super-tight movement mechanics are on-point, arguably even improving on the titles it draws inspiration from. The strafing feels natural, allowing you to dance around the battlefield with the fluidity and grace of a ballerina. The weapon lineup is solid, each gun beautifully crafted and animated with meaty sound effects, making combat an extremely satisfying and visceral experience. Everything just clicks.

Level design: A well-crafted FPS consists of more than the sum of it's gameplay mechanics, and level design is arguably one of the more important cogs in the machinery. The art direction is outstanding, the texture work is beautiful. Areas are large and sprawling, yet they maintain a consistent sense of progression, guiding the player through one stunning set-piece after another, while still retaining the feel of a more open-ended design philosophy. Secrets are cleverly hidden in every corner. Players used to secret-hunting in classic FPS will naturally come across most of them, but there are still a handful that will catch you off-guard.

Atmosphere: This is where most retro-FPS fail in my opinion, in the establishing of a consistent atmosphere to compliment it's gameplay. Not Dusk, they nailed it from the get go. The setting, themes and visual elements merge beautifully with the awesome soundtrack to create a memorable and unique atmosphere. The game oozes with a Lovecraftian sense of dread and foreboding from the first level. I had moments of feeling genuinely unsettled, which is a rare thing these days. The game demonstrates it's competence in this area especially well during some of the later enemy reveals. I can't think of any recent title that does enemy reveals in such a dramatic, terrifying and cool way as Dusk does.

Music: The soundtrack is nothing short of superb. I was already familiar with Hulshults work from Rise of the Triad 2013 and Quake Champions, and his work on Dusk clearly demonstrates that he's undoubtedly one of the best video game composers in recent times. The music ranges from hauntingly beautiful ambiance to brick-shitting terror and adrenaline-fueled combat anthems that makes you feel like a true badass, and the overarching gritty industrial theme remains consistent throughout, clearly drawing inspiration from Trent Reznors work on Quake, yet standing out enough to become an iconic soundtrack in it's own right.

To summarize, this game caught me completely off-guard and ended up becoming one of my all-time favorites, and is undoubtedly one of the best retro-FPS titles out there.

Make no mistake, Dusk is not merely emulating the titans of oldschool FPS, it stands proudly beside them as an equal.

As a huge fan of retro FPS games, I honestly do not have a single complaint. Dusk is an old school First Person Shooter, similar to 90's era Doom, Quake, and Duke Nukem 3D.

The Good
 
•	Movement speed is FAST, so you can dodge enemy projectiles instead of hiding behind chest high walls, and make use of your circle strafing skills.
•	Lots of different types of enemies, including crazed lumberjacks, fireball throwing cultists, shotgun wielding scarecrows, and many more demonic creatures.
•	Use all the classic guns, including dual pistols, dual shotguns, super shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, crossbow (bolts penetrate enemies for multi-kills), grenade launcher and rocket launcher. Plus dual sickles or a sword if you want to melee.
•	You can carry all the weapons simultaneously because fun > realism.
•	Excellent level design, featuring maze like layouts, lots of verticality, plenty of bounce pads, coloured doors and keys, enemies waiting to ambush you when you press buttons, and secrets to find.
•	Health is restored by collecting medkits, which I always prefer instead of regeneration.
•	A couple of powerups will help you take out large hordes: increased firing speed and Superhot style “time only moves when you move”.
•	Heavy metal soundtrack is a good match for the fast paced action.
•	I didn’t have any crashes or framerate problems. Controls are fully rebindable.

The Bad 

•	Story mode is a bit short, as I completed it in 7 hours. There is an endless mode, but the maps are small so I don’t anticipate playing them for a long time.

The Recommendation
 
If you like single player First Person Shooters, you MUST play Dusk.

[i]DUSK[/i] harkens back to an older age of shooters, one that’s been making a resurgence thanks to the modern interpretations of [i]Wolfenstein & DOOM[/i]. Whereas those titles adopt design choices both new and old, [i]DUSK[/i] differs in that it wants you to think it was ripped straight out of the past. From the blocky visuals to the breakneck gameplay,  [i]DUSK[/i] is a retro shooter through and through, and we’re all the better for it.

I don’t think [i]DUSK[/i] has any particular selling point as much as it succeeds from the sum of its parts. Visuals, story, gameplay, nothing here is truly exceptional, but it's all of great quality and seamlessly blends into create a creepy yet exhilarating FPS. [i]David Szymanski[/i] has done a fantastic job here, creating a fast paced shooter inspired by the greats, which now stands alongside its inspirations in quality.

[h1]Dusk, Pennsylvania[/h1] 
Don’t let the dated look fool you, the artistic direction is amazing. [i]DUSK[/i] approaches everything with simplicity and efficiency, and it's extremely apparent in the graphics. Everything has a basic blocky look to it. It's all easily readable, yet it makes the world very imposing and intimidating, being made of rough shapes. Enemies in particular are a highlight, their jagged forms make them uncanny and unnerving as they approach you, creating a delightfully creepy experience. 

The world of [i]DUSK[/i] is completed by the striking use of colours and lights. The world is drab and bleak, the dullened greens and browns really sell that, and it allows the more evocative splashes of colour to stand out, mainly the strong reds of blood marks or torchlights. The environments feel dark and gritty that gives the world a sinister vibe. Without giving anything away, the way the visuals twist and contort over the game's duration is excellent, nothing stays predictable for long.

The visuals are also incredibly customizable thanks to the massive breadth of graphics options. You can make this game appear far cleaner, more pixelated,  change the colour tints, the list goes on. While I’d recommend the default look, the level of personalisation available is truly insane and deeply appreciated.

[i]DUSK[/i]’s delightful visuals help convey a simplistic ghastly narrative. The game is broken into three acts as you delve into the mysterious cultist town of Dusk. Each act brings a different feel, themed around certain enemies and environments, but they all flow into each other beautifully. The gameplay is enjoyable enough without these details, yet their inclusion allows [i]DUSK[/i] to stand out from retro shooters.

[h1]”Kill the Intruder…”[/h1]
One of the greatest aspects of [i]DUSK[/i] is the pacing. From the moment you hit play, everything feels fast and frantic, yet controllable, maintaining that feeling of chaotic escalation until the finale. I love how quickly you jump into [i]DUSK[/i], no time is wasted. I love how the controls are so basic, yet feel immediately responsive and familiar, even to someone like myself who isn’t super experienced with retro shooters. 

The gunplay excels due to a good balance between effective weaponry and a speedy player character.  Weapon variety is decent, there's nothing you haven’t seen before, but it's a good set of guns for every situation. I found myself wishing for a bit more to play with, I unlocked all the guns in the first hour or so, finding nothing new and instead having these weapons taken away at the end of each act wasn’t enjoyable.

Movement is a bit more special, you move fast and jump high, allowing you to seamlessly zip around levels. There are plenty of jump pads and power ups for the surprisingly vertical environments. The best arenas consist of you speeding from place to place killing anyone who gets in your way, a great gameplay loop. 

Of course the shooting wouldn’t be exhilitrating without any challenges to overcome. Thankfully, [i]DUSK[/i] offers an impressive variety of enemies to keep your head in the fight at all times. You’ve got a great mixture of monsters that get up and personal and attack from far away, as well as a few that employ sneaky or unpredictable tactics. Thanks to their terrifying designs, the larger threats are always easy to pick out in hordes, making it easier to plan who you want to take out first while on the go.

[h1]From The Foothills to The Facilities[/h1]
The gunplay wouldn’t be complete without a series of memorable and varied levels to shoot through. Each act of [i]DUSK[/i] has a unique theme as you voyage deeper into town. You start off in the quaint yet eerie outskirts, consisting of forestry and farms. As you get closer to town, environments become more populated with both structures and enemies.

The ways these levels and acts flow into each other is excellent, taking you a number of exciting locations that escalate naturally. However, I do think the middle act is weaker than the others, it’s filled with just a few too many generic building environments. It conveys the demonic town narrative quite well, but it does result in a few forgettable levels.

The variety of these levels is truly impressive. Levels can range from boxed in to massive open spaces, or horizontal landscapes to vertical towers seamlessly. Every corner you turn has the chance of throwing something unpredictable in your face. The last act in particular throws some crazy environments into the fray, making the game's finale feel so wild compared to everything that came before. You’re constantly shifting between new locations, warping your perspective on reality, which really gives off that ‘descending into insanity’ feel.

As with many retro shooters, [i]DUSK[/i] has a litany of secrets to uncover in each level, ranging from powerful weapons appearing early, health boosters, bars of soap, and occasionally, secret levels. They’re what you’d expect from a retro shooter, although I would’ve preferred slightly more exciting rewards. I thought the way they were employed in the environment was well thought out, making hunting for secrets enjoyable, backtracking is encouraged thanks to smartly placed portals. I often had a second sweep through levels to look for goodies, however I never went fully into secret hunting, mainly due to the sheer size of later levels.

A few levels did unfortunately employ some cheap deaths, such as pitfalls. One particularly long level ends with a boss fight on a series of platforms, where any slip results in immediate death. Any failed attempt became greatly frustrating, especially when compared to the rest of the game. These instances were few, but annoying due to a lack of checkpoints.

[h1]8/10[/h1]
[i]DUSK[/i] is one of the purest homages I’ve ever played. It's actively staying faithful to the era its emulating, yet not afraid to utilise modern technology or design trends. While at times I wish what was here had been pushed a bit further, [i]DUSK[/i] is first and foremost an impressive, exciting and complete experience, that doesn’t waste a moment of your time. It's certainly a great time for any fan of retro shooters, especially for those who also enjoy horror.

One of the best shooters of all time, full stop.

- Excellent gunplay and movement
- Creative level design that only gets stronger the further along you get
- Unique enemies that change every episode as to not get stale
- Killer music by the king of classic FPS composers Andrew Hulshult

And that's about it as far as complaints go, Dusk is incredible and you owe it to yourself to play it even if old school FPS is something you have never delved into before.

I loved it, and then I didn't. I remember the exact moment when I became bored and playing started feeling like a chore, but I'm not completely sure why. It feels like nothing really has changed, but... maybe that's the reason? Let's just start at the beginning. Because the beginning is amazing.

[h1]Into the SATAN[/h1]
Yeah, the game's early hours are a hodgepodge of your stereotypical isolated village with a dark secret tropes and I'm here for that. Weird dungeons hidden under barns, farmer dudes with chainsaws, klansmen-style cultists; and you get to blast those sonnuvas with an arsenal of familiar weapons with a twist. A pistol? Why not two pistols? A shotgun? Why not two shotguns? A super shotgun? Okay, that's already perfect. 

The level design's pretty tight at first. It flows, has secrets of varying complexity to find, and it invites you to delve deeper. What's going on here? How far does this go? And who's the mysterious voice that keeps talking to you?

New weapons here, a boss or two there, slow descend into the heart of madness makes you breeze through the first episode. At this point, the game is pretty hard to put down.

[h1]Episode 7: Somehow, Duskdude returned[/h1]
This is probably where I should mention that this game was in Early Access for a while, and was released one episode at a time. Nothing wrong with that by itself; but it's pretty clear that the episodes were meant to be fun experiences in their own scope. So the pacing is made to fit individual episodes. 

What this means is - for example - once you reach the end of Episode 1, you'll have found every single weapon there is. The Sword, a weapon you get naturally in Episode 3, can only be found in a secret - but it's there, and I found it. You'll be at your most powerful relatively early on, and the game needs to make sure the challenge remains consistent; but it also (rightfully) wants to add new enemies in latter episodes. What should be their strength level?

[h1]Diabolical Industrial Complex[/h1]
As you enter Episode 2, you notice that all your weapons are gone. That's alright, you'll just have to build up your again. This time, you're entering some kind of strange military themed installation, and the weird demonic stuff takes a bit of a back seat.

...and it's just not as interesting, unfortunately.

A few enemies get swapped out for new, more thematically-appropriate ones; but the variety remains somewhat low. On average, you'll probably encounter 3-4 types of enemies in a given level, with an occasional surprise.

When I reached the 8th level of Episode 2 - the Erebus Reactor - I realised I'm really forcing myself to play. The level is a bit of a mess - involves climbing, collecting keycards, opening a chain of doors, all in a large, open area - with an annoying lava pool that's relatively easy to fall into. So I had to redo this part a little too often for my liking, even with quicksaving.

[h1]Back to Hell[/h1]
And unfortunately, the game failed to reignite my interest afterwards. It did get better, but eventually I just had to shelve it. Even reaching and beating half of the final episode didn't do much for me, even if it was somewhat better then the second one.

Since the game was in Early Access, the achievement data probably isn't very reliable (some might've played when the game was "IN" but then forgot about it) - but if we assume that it's somewhat truthful, then other players had a similar experience. 46% of players beat the first episode, and 26% beat the second. Most of these players beat the third too, at 22%. Those are pretty decent numbers, considering the game has 20k reviews, so hey, lots of people clearly enjoy it.

It's a shame. I loved the beginning, but then I got bored. That doesn't usually happen for me when it comes to boomer shooters. The only one I can recall that had this effect was... Amid Evil? Oh, that's by the same [strike]developer[/strike] publisher? I guess our styles don't match. I respect the work, though.

[b]tl;dr: This game is a ton of fun right now and has a lot to offer if you enjoy arena style shooters or have been feeling an itch for a good, single player, retro fps![/b]

[b][i][u]-I am going to avoid spoilers in this review / explanation-[/u][/i][/b]

[h1]A "Quick" Summary:[/h1]
[b][i](I'll go into more detail about most of these points later in the review)[/i][/b]
I'm loving everything about this game! I pre-ordered it a while back ([i]before[/i] early access) and have been playing the single and multiplayer as 2 separate games. Right now, there are 2 episodes, the multiplayer, and 2 endless arenas to play with. And episode 3 and endless arena 3 are on the way, so the game is not 100% complete, but still has plenty to play with as it stands ([i]I have 90 hours in it so far[/i]). With that being said, DUSK takes what made games like Quake and DOOM great and makes them its own. You can play it fast and kill everything, play it passive and let everything live, or slow it down and look for secrets (there is a lot of them). The levels feel great and look great and each offer something different while being simple enough to get through with sometimes having multiple ways to complete them. Some of these levels have a bit of a horror element to them as well leading to some pretty tense and scary moments. Movement is fast and the weapons feel great and are perfect for the game. Combat can be hectic at times, but everything feels fair. I highly recommend this game.

[h1]Story:[/h1]
The story [i]so far[/i] is: You play as "Dusk Dude", a treasure hunter captured by demonic cultists. You must escape and kill them all. [i]Simple[/i]. As you progress you discover some truths about what's really been going on.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
[b][i](for now I will just talk about the single player, as it is the main feature of DUSK, however, a lot of this applies to the multiplayer as well)[/i][/b]

[b][u]MOVEMENT:[/u][/b] DUSK plays how you want it to. It can be played very fast by use of bunny-hopping or explosive jumping, or taken slower for those who wish to do so. The important thing is that you are in control. You have complete freedom in your movement both on the ground and in the air. Having this freedom allows you to dodge enemy's and get around the levels as you please and feel good while doing it. 

[b][u]BASIC WEAPONS:[/u][/b] There are technically 10 weapons in this game, but one is a special melee weapon seldom used. The main 9 weapons are nothing too fancy, but are perfect for the setting and theme. They feel extremely responsive, sound great, and all serve a unique purpose. I won't go into these purposes too much as its better to learn from playing, but they are pretty much what you would expect of them. Pistols for small enemy's, shotguns for getting in your enemy's faces or for needing high damage, rifles for medium and long ranges, explosives for crowds or bosses and for jumping to hard to reach places, a special crossbow which can shoot through walls and allow the player to hover if shot down, and your trusty sickles for when you're in a pinch. The guns follow the retro trend of not needing to manually reload or worry about magazines and a very quick to switch to and use. 

[b][u]IMPROVISED WEAPONS:[/u][/b] In DUSK you can pick up most small objects in the game, and each of these objects can be thrown to do different damages depending on what they are. It makes for interesting fights and allows the player to save ammo if needed.

[b][u]PICKUPS:[/u][/b] There are various health, armor (armor is called "morale" in DUSK), ammo, weapons, and power-ups placed throughout each level. Some are clearly presented as you move through them and others are hidden to reward exploration. Enemy's can also drop small amounts of health, morale, and ammo as well. These pickups feel very well placed and provide a good reason to explore as you can obtain some weapons early in the game.

[b][u]COMBAT:[/u][/b] No crazy AI in this game. If they see you, they will chase you. Rushing into a room guns blazing is the way this game was made to be played!

[b][u]SOUNDTRACK:[/u][/b] Badass soundtrack that is dynamic on most levels. No complaints here. Most of the sound design feels very modern, while still having some old school-esque sounds throughout the game.

[h1]Multiplayer:[/h1]
The multiplayer is awesome, but it is an afterthought or an add-on to the single player and is still in fairly early stages. It is a standard arena style PvP setup with (at the time of this review) only 1 game mode, free for all. However, more game modes are planned (CTF, TDM,etc). To start, you NEED to be fast and have a basic understanding of DUSK's movement to do [i]well[/i] in it. Or else you are an easy target for everyone else. But, with that being said, the multiplayer has a low skill floor and high skill ceiling. Anyone can easily get a hang of the movement and weapons within an hour or 2 and can take those skills very far. It is an arena style fps done right!

[h1]Graphics and Aesthetics:[/h1]
I figured I would toss this in at the end as it shouldn't be a [i]major[/i] selling point in my opinion. But this game is very 90's. What you see in the screenshots is what you get. But don't let its graphics make your choice on this game, it is very tastefully used and is very much part of its charm. 

[h1]Future Features:[/h1]
There is still a lot to be added to DUSK during its time in and out of early access. A SDK is currently in the works with planned workshop support, more game modes and features for multiplayer, potential co-op after it leaves early access, and episode 3 are the main things to note. But I'm sure many other small features and tweaks will be added along the way.

And that's about it! I'm loving this game so far and am looking forward to episode 3 within the next couple of months! I don't want to talk about enemy types or specifics of the levels just yet as those are best experienced by playing the game and are potential spoilers. Maybe after episode 3 comes out and I can look at everything as a whole I will add a spoiler section and talk about those.

[b][i]-BTW, This game is probably not going to go on sale anytime soon (if AT ALL) as to avoid the "I'll pick it up when it's on sale" excuse. It will also always be $20 no matter how much more content is added. This is a dev choice that has been stated multiple times on their Discord as well as on their 2018 announcement: "Nope. $20 then, $20 now, $20 forever." I think it is very much worth the price for the time I got (and am still getting) out of it. I have gotten 90+ hours between the single and multiplayer (40 single, 50 multi). It miiiight go on sale eventually, but I would not count on it. If this game looks appealing to you, PICK IT UP!!-[/i][/b]

This was (if I'm remembering right) one of the first of the wave of retro boomer shooters. That might make you think it's a little more generic, a little less creative, than the games that came later.

You'd be wrong.

The level design here is immensely creative and fun - almost like a tour of the best custom Doom/Quake levels. They also manage to avoid a lot of the pitfalls of classic level design (like the over-reliance on mazes) while still feeling believably retro. I really want to say more, but I don't want to spoil some of the cooler sections, so I'll just say: It's great!

The art & environmental design is phenomenal, too. There are some scenic moments in this game that made me gasp out loud (and then hammer the screenshot button). Stuff that I would expect in a Kitty Horrorshow game, not a rambunctious boomer shooter. I never knew quite what to expect when rounding the next corner.

And, naturally, the gameplay is basically fun-in-a-can. It absolutely feels like one of the classic 90s shooters, in a good way - it even has bunny hopping. It's admittedly nothing you haven't seen before, but hey - if it ain't broke, don't fix it. Dusk is already doing plenty of unique stuff elsewhere, so I think keeping the gameplay classic (but very polished) was a good move.

If you like boomer shooters at all, this is a must play.

Games that are meant to be callbacks or love letters to earlier legends fall into a dicey gambit, since the comparison to its predecessor comes in the form both of how much it evokes the original and what it does differently - Or not similarly enough. This leads to Dusk, a shooter that doesn’t need much viewing to decipher what games had inspired its look, feel and speed. Despite such clear inspiration, Dusk manages to be its own entity instead of being a mere love letter for the sake of lazy comparisons. The fact it’s also fun and plays fantastically doesn’t hurt, either.

It’s always hard to explain why a game feels ‘good’ unless you can actually sit down to try it yourself, and Dusk is no exception. While the game plays very quickly and initially feels loose and and unruly, there’s a certain surgical precision amidst all the madness - Once you get a grasp of the mobility and aiming along with it. It will most certainly take a few levels to get adjusted to the speed of movement, but excluding a few charging enemy types, it’s comical how your character can run dozens of laps around enemies and they’re unable to do a thing about it. This is most certainly an asset when surrounded at all angles or facing a firing squad, so the real learning curve is learning how to zip about like a madman but also be able to hit a target. While other shooters prompts the player to prioritize targets to avoid getting killed, Dusk encourages lots of rapid hit-and-run warfare inbetween bobbing out of cover. While playing carefully does get the job done, the game excels when played like a deranged speedfreak, hopping around the environment and never letting go of movement keys.

At the time of writing, Dusk has two episodes available to play that features rather pleasantly deceptive level design, and I don’t mean that as an insult. The early levels are somewhat linear with expected side paths to find secrets, with later levels becoming larger and more complicated to navigate. In both cases, they’re still quite small if you were run from start to finish without stopping, but they ‘feel’ bigger during skirmishes when dodging enemy fire and returning your own. Navigating each map would certainly be ire inducing if it wasn’t for the speedy character movement, a blessing in itself when trying to dig everywhere for secrets and having to backtrack. This leads to my only current, big issue with Dusk so far; enemies spawns are set and limited, but even with some levels littering over a hundred bad guys, enemy placement occurs in occasional pockets, individuals or large battles - I can’t help but feel like there isn’t enough combat which sounds bizarre for a game like this, especially with said big battles ending almost as quickly as they begin if one plays offensively. My other minor gripe is that in a couple levels your flashlight becomes broken due to a long fall, which drops visibility in a game that already loves putting the player into dark areas. This would be a fine way of raising tension for the sake of the creepy, eerie environments while being beset by baddies, but these lightless sections are just inconveniences rather than a set piece. Bumping around in the dark and using pistols as temporary flashes of light isn’t much fun, but luckily this element is used sparingly.

If those are my only major gripes excluding some personal issues of my own (like the aesthetic jump from episode one to two), then it should be clear how Dusk succeeds as a shooter. It plays fast, great and the level design lends itself to being quick to navigate through along with not being gargantuan mazes. I finished the current two episodes in just over four and a half hours, and while my comat fixin’ could be solved by the Endless mode, it is a bit shallow in terms of being a cramped arena where loops are run over and over. I most certainly am looking forward to the final product of Dusk along with the third and final(?) episode, and it goes without saying that I can give it a solid recommendation. 

(Early Access note: My playthrough didn’t merit major technical issues despite its developmental state. At worst, I had encountered moments of sound dropping due to multiple sound effects playing at once and lighting bugs when moving some objects from lit to unlit areas. The game is very much functional and stable at this time. And good - Did I mention it was good?)
