As someone who grew up playing games like Quake, I can safely say this game outclasses its own inspiration. Without exaggeration, Dusk is easily one of the best shooters I've played in a long time. I'm usually not too interested in "revival" shooters as too often I feel they lean too hard on the things that made their inspirations great without stepping too far out of that comfort zone. Dusk definitely does a lot to set it apart from what it's aesthetic and gameplay are built off of. 

Something I really hate about old shooters is key hunting. For instance, as influential as it was, I consider Duke Nukem 3D to be one of the worst examples of this. Levels with a massive scale are only hindered by progression being gated by keys in such sequestered areas of the map. When I played Dusk in early access, I was afraid it would fall into this same trap. While the game does use the good old red blue and yellow key system, I never found it a chore to search for any of them. Many of the levels are very large scale, but designed in a way that makes key hunting less of a chore and more something that happens naturally. 

It's hard for me to go into detail about everything I love about Dusk because there's just so much to love about it. Every episode has its own motif but not once does it ever start to feel samey. All of the weapons have just the right amount of oomf to them. The sound design is flawless and this game is one of the few that has a soundtrack that stands out from the game it's in. It's seriously that good. All I can say is that you definitely shouldn't write this off as "just another revival shooter". There's so much more to it than that.

My complaints are very few. One of which being that while almost all the weapons feel good to use, one in particular was so finicky and inconsistent that I basically never used it unless I knew it was going to hit something. This being the mortar launcher. For some reason the grenades it shoots feel like they're shot on a delay. This has something to do with your momentum and I'm sure there's a rhyme and reason to it, but I couldn't figure it out after many attempts at using it, so I ended up not using it for the majority of my playthrough. The riveter, which is basically a rocket launcher, is much better and feels like it can fill the same role as the mortar launcher 9 times out of ten.

Another is one specific enemy type. In episode 2, you fight a boss called Mama. It's one of the most fun boss fights in the entire game because half the fight is how you navigate the arena. In the next level however a new enemy type appears called the cowgirl which is basically the same as the boss with a third of the health but the same amount of damage. This enemy is incredibly irritating to fight. In the boss fight, it's just you vs her which makes the fight feel fun and fair. But the enemy type is just annoying to fight most of the time. She's extremely thin, and on Cero Miedo (the second hardest difficulty) she can kill you in about 2-3 hits. This wouldn't be an issue if not for the fact that you rarely encounter one by themselves. Often she'll be surrounded by other enemies and at worst she'll have another cowgirl with her. When you're trying to avoid the gunfire of multiple enemies and her grenades it becomes very stressful and difficult to deal with, and her hitbox being so small is where the problem is most apparent.

Despite how cheap it feels, however, it never feels like you're fighting an unfair battle. By the time you get to her, you're more than well equipped to dispatch her. And I don't believe this game does the Doom thing of making pickups appear less on higher difficulties, so you never truly feel like you're running low on something to get you out of that pinch.

-Spoiler territory-
The game's final level has such a sweet taste but such a sour aftertaste. The final stage has two bosses. The first one is Jakob and his fight is an absolute blast. It's basically a competitive 1v1 arena shooter match. It's a match against another person of the same size, with the same kit, and the same mobility. Even if it's basically a bot match with a hard bot it's still a ton of fun. 

However, Jakob is the penultimate boss. The real boss is Nyarlathotep and he's not nearly as fun to fight. The boss arena is big but there's only two small platforms you can stand on without taking damage. Fall below them and you'll sustain damage constantly until you jump back up to the main platform. This wouldn't be an issue if not for the fact that some of the attacks the boss does covers both of the areas you can stand, and if you're not in the middle with really specific timing you'll get hit, and even if you don't you'll often fall in the gap below and take damage anyway. It's a lot less, at least, but still kind of irritating.

The boss's gimmick is that cracks will eventually start to form on the walls behind him. Until you break these open, he's invulnerable. And after taking enough hits, he becomes invincible again until you break another wall. This would be fine if the timing for the cracks was consistent, but it isn't. It took me several attempts to beat him, and in each one of those the cracks appeared at completely random times. The first one would sometimes appear instantly, and other times it'd take up to 30 seconds. This wouldn't be a problem except the boss can still damage you while invulnerable, and on higher difficulties it takes about 3 hits before you die. 

It doesn't feel unfair but it definitely feels cheap when I'm having to dodge damage in such a tight space while I wait for the game to tell me it's okay to attack the boss while it gives me no indication of whether or not it's going to be in 2 seconds or 20. 

Other than that, there are no other flaws I can think of that are worth mentioning. And even then, those are such minor complaints when compared to how much the game gets right. I highly recommend you check it out, even if old school shooters aren't totally your thing.

You've heard a lot of good things about this game and have seen the 98% positive reviews. I'm here to share some details to so you can determine if it's your cup of tea or not.

I've finished the game multiple times (twice in Steam, maybe 4 times non-steam) and have also played a few Community Made maps. Just couldn't get enough of the game. So with all that, here's what I have to share.

[h1]Short[/h1]
DUSK takes inspiration from  90s shooters such as Quake, DOOM, Half-Life, etc. It's got a fast paced gameplay, emphasis on speed, movement and shooting with an arsenal of 10 weapons that you carry at once, all put together with a rich 90s aesthetic, great enemy design, fantastic level design and a kickass soundtrack to go with it.


[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Graphics are designed with the 90s aesthetic and it works! It's not a generic Low Poly model that you seem to find in every game asset store, no. It's designed specifically to look like a 90s game, with enough details and geometry to look and feel from that era without being ugly or lazy. Textures are not just plain colors and you'll find that actual work has been put into everything to look exactly the way it does now.
This is packed with some newer technology settings like Post Processing and Dynamic Lights/Shadows. It also has settings to make the game feel older, with options to make the game look more pixelated or add a color Theme. There's a lot of options to tweak with to get that specialized old-look that you'd personally want. You can also disable all of that to make it look more sharp, crisp and modern.


[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay is fast paced with solid movement controls and an arsenal of 10 weapons, all of which can be "fast switched". So DOOM/Quake players will feel right at home.
Each weapon is unique. In a game like DOOM/Quake, you might find yourself using only a few of the weapons or having some weaker weapons become obsolete when better guns are acquired. Unless of coarse you are [b]FORCED[/b] to use them all like in DOOM Eternal where in higher difficulties, you are FORCED to use Grenades for Cacodemons, Plasma Cannon for Shield enemies, etc. if you want to actually deal damage. DUSK [b]doesn't force you[/b] to "weapon switch", it instead [b]encourages[/b] you to do so.

[list]
Here, weapons don't have different mods or anything. Instead, there are 10 weapons [b]designed specifically[/b] to be [b]different[/b] and [b]unique[/b] in their own way, which makes each of them great for different situations. For example:
[*] The Dual Shotguns have a high rate of fire and damage; so if you need constant fire at medium range, they're perfect.
[*] The Double Barrel gives a much higher damage output at the cost of a much lower range and rate of fire.
[*] The Hunting Rifle acts as a Railgun, accurate as f*ck, great for any range and can kill most enemies with 1-2 shots.
[*] While the Crossbow feels similar to Hunting Rifle, it is actually different. It deals less damage but instead penetrates through enemies. So if any amount of enemies are standing behind each other, you can fire one bolt and it will go through all of them. Add the fact that it can kill most weaker enemies and you've got a deadly weapon for crowd control.[/list]

I can go on but you understand the point. Each weapon is different and is used for different situations. There's no one to FORCE you to use them in such ways, but as you play more and on higher difficulties, you'll naturally start to use them like that. This alone makes this game's Gunplay much more enjoyable for me than Eternal's forced methods.


[h1]Enemies[/h1]
The enemy roster is varied. There are [b]NO hit-scanning enemies[/b] and each one is different and fun to fight. Harder enemies are introduced the further you get into the campaign and the Difficulty level affects not their Health, but mostly their Projectile Speeds and Damage. So you won't find incredibly spongy enemies at higher difficulties but instead, enemies harder to dodge and fight. Which is a plus and doesn't end you up with something like Tom Clancy's Division, which had you emptying 50 rifle rounds into an enemy's head before they died.


[h1]Level Design[/h1]
The level design is fantastic! There are 3 acts in the game, consisting of multiple levels and not only are the [b]acts[/b] different from each other but also [b]each level[/b] is different and distinguishable from the others too! There's also some good [b]Environmental Story Telling[/b] here and there.

In terms of gameplay they work great! There's a good level of [b]verticality[/b] to them, each room/area feels like an [b]Arena[/b] designed to fight in, enemy placement is good and not cheap and encounters get harder the further you get into the game, not by bad levels or an ambush of dozens of enemies, but by [b]clever level design and enemy placement[/b]. Every map is also filled with lots of [b]small-big secrets[/b] that you can find, encouraging exploring and secret-hunting.

The only issue I've had with the Level Design is that some secrets [b]give you some of the more powerful weapons at the beginning[/b] which can make things a lot easier than they should be.

The game encourages [b]Speedruns[/b]. Each level has a counter that shows you how much time it took you to finish it and even a Developer Time is included which you can beat! One important thing is that if you'd want to set a world record, you can speed through a lot of the areas and no enemy encounter is really a Hard Stop for you. A lot of doors and paths are open or can be opened without completely clearing areas and the maps are not completely sealed ([b]intentionally[/b]) so you can use your own tricks to skip almost any encounter if needed.


[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is the same routine for a Boomer Shooter. There's enough of it to motivate you to keep playing and find out what the hell is going on but not too much to bore you or ruin your imagination. No sequence takes away control from you or takes you into a cinematic/third person camera.
There's also a comic (in the Deluxe Edition) which sheds more light into the world, so you can also read that if you want.


[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
My god the soundtrack! It's on par with Mick Gordon's work and I personally enjoy it more than DOOM's. I've got the soundtrack and have listened to it more times than I can count throughout the years.
Each track is different from the others and yet they all feel part of the same soundtrack. All tracks feel like a roller coaster ride, having their ups and downs throughout the track never feeling stale.
I have no idea what makes good music so I can't really dive into the technical aspects. I'll just stress it again that it has been one of my most favorite soundtracks since the first day I heard it in-game.


[h1]The Bad & Conclusion[/h1]
I only had two major problems with this game: the "Secrets" one (mentioned in Level Design) and the lack of higher Difficulty Levels. There are only 5 difficulty levels:
[list]
[*] Accessible (for any skill level)
[*] Go Easy (Easy)
[*] I Can Take It (Normal)
[*] Cero Miedo (Hard)
[*] DUSKMARE (Hard with 1 Hit = death)
[/list]
You can also play on any difficulty level with "Intruder Mode" which makes you start each level with only basic melee. You'd have to find and pick up your guns in the map again .

If you're not a big fan of DUSKMARE Difficulty, you'll probably only be able to play the campaign 3 times.
After that, you can play the "Endless" mode, try to find all the secrets, unlock all achievements for maps, check out the Custom Levels created by the players or the PVP Multiplayer (no idea about the player-base).
So the amount of replayability depends on your taste. I personally wish there were more high Difficulty Levels before DUSKMARE.

Still, this is a tightly crafted game that deserves all the positive reviews it has gotten. If you're a boomer shooter or want to experience a modern one, I [b]fully recommend[/b] this game.
I love this game, aesthetic choices are top, atmosphere is unique, and the soundtrack is one of my favourites in any game i've ever played. Buy it.

Dusk is a game that I wish I played the moment it came out. Not because I found it to be a groundbreaking masterpiece, but because it would really benefit from not having any sort of pre-existing expectations. If you've been hanging around any sort of gaming community, you probably heard more than a few people recommending Dusk or praise it as the second coming of Shotgun Jesus. It's kinda like your friend hyping up a joke as the funniest thing he ever heard, nothing can be funny enough to live up to that!

That said, Dusk is a really good game regardless, especially if you consider that it was largely made by one guy. Everything you'll find here is solid, though rarely more than that. First episode in particular doesn't put Dusk's best foot forward. Much of it feels someone making a spiritual successor to Redneck Rampage, with its secluded woods, dilapidated houses, and rusted industrial areas. It feels standard, like something you've played or seen a dozen times already.

However, Dusk gets so much more unique and creative with its levels as you go along. One mission puts you in the "Escher Labs," which lives up to its name. A generic level suddenly breaks your expectations as the layout shifts and you're put into rooms with nonsensical and confusing layouts (in a good way). There's even a neat reference to Constatine's Mansion from Thief in there. Logically, episode 3 peaks in terms of creativity. Suiddenly you're exploring an industrial cathedral, an underground city with sunken ruins beneath it, dark catacombs that are being consumed by some sort of flesh and guts. It's cool as hell and often shows off that Szymanski is a master of horror and atmospheric sound design.

I've been talking largely about the maps so far, but that's for a reason. Dusk is at its best when you're exploring and fighting through the more interesting settings it has to offer because the rest of the game never really breaks out of that "standard" mold.

Almost all enemies in the game are fairly unimaginative. Despite having well over a dozen different, it feels like there's just 2. One is a melee enemy that just runs at you - Leatherneck, Rat, Scientist, Wendigo, Priestess, Cart Dog. All of these are just the same enemy, with only Cart Dog doing something interesting, as them speeding up into you makes them more of a threat than other melee enemies, who will stop in place to hit you, which makes it painfully easy to avoid their attacks. That's when they're not falling victim to the awful AI pathing when any sort of complex geometry is involved. 

Ranged enemies are much the same. Some of them run at you and the shoot, others wander around and then shoot. All of which is typically nullified by strafe jumping. In terms of difficulty, it makes the game fairly easy even on Cero Miedo, since you never have to put much thought into dodging or positioning, especially with most levels either providing generous space for strafe jumping or corridors to fill with fire. But difficulty aside, it just makes most encounters far too basic, since there is only so much room for varied combat scenarios when you essentially have 2 basic enemies.

The arsenal of weapons doesn't help, as the only remotely interesting weapon you have is a crossbow that can pierce walls and enemies, while also allowing for minor "crossbow jumps" with its minor knockback. The rest is as basic as it gets. Shotgun, super shotgun, pistols that serve as a bad machinegun, a proper machinegun, sniper rifle, rocket launcher, and grenade launcher. There are also two melee weapons, and while the sword is quite strong, both are virtually pointless. Not that the other weapons have a defined use. I've beaten the game twice and I went through most of it with just a shotgun. For some that's great, everyone loves a good boomstick, but I prefer it when enemy patterns and your arsenal encourage at least some basic decision making during the fights.

Finally it's worth mentioning the story and music. The former is predictably dull, but throws out a cool twist at the end that recontextualizes mindless ripping and tearing in a very interesting way. The latter is much more notable however. Any FPS fan has heard of Hulshult at this point and for a good reason, he can really put out some great GUGIDA GUGIDA GUGIDA music that goes exceptionally well with the aforementioned ripping and tearing. Dusk in particular kinda felt similar to his Quake Champions stuff, and I'm not complaining.

This is probably way too negative right now for a review that has a blue thumb on it, but I do still feel like Dusk is just a really good game that any FPS fan should buy and/or play (poverty is a bitch, so do what you gotta do). At its best, Dusk is great, and its worst, it's usually just solid, and you can't say that about that many FPS games, especially most things that the triple A side of the industry has been putting out. Also, if you're a Serious Sam or Painkiller fan, you probably can't even read this review, let alone care about the negative things I've said, so if you just want to blast some monsters and hump walls to find secrets, Dusk is a must-have.

[h1]Retro FPS renaissance[/h1]
The transcendent, the one and only, DUSK.  A retro FPS created with seemingly endless creativity and design intricate enough to earn the game its rightful place among the classics like Quake or Blood. By the end of 2018 when DUSK came out, retro FPSes were still relatively few in number. I believe the game’s success paved the way towards retro FPS genre becoming nowadays one of the most prolific types among indie games in general. All that for a good reason.

[b]The intruder[/b]
Let’s get the classic game references out of the way early – in terms of graphics DUSK is best compared to Quake with its chunky 3D visuals. The game is also widely compared to Doom because of the general atmosphere of this title, as well as coloured keys and doors being a core mechanic. Admittedly, DUSK evidently draws from these titles, however the game goes way beyond a pale imitation by taking the formula in its own unique direction – it’s a retro FPS, albeit one evidently made in 2018.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2792091706[/url]
With that hurdle out of the way, it’s time for the menacing title card. The first sight afterwards is a group of 3 chainsaw-wielding maniacs charging at Duskdude. As you dispatch the enemies with game’s signature sickle in each hand, you come to realise that your character was hanging in decrepit basement with meat hooks lodged in his back just seconds ago. It takes DUSK about 15 seconds to properly establish the atmosphere of mystery and danger and it only keeps building upon this foundation. Beside small hints and a text bar at the end of each episode, DUSK offers precious little in terms of story, although it really doesn’t need one. Fluid gameplay, atmospheric soundtrack and visually distinct level design join together to make the player leap into the fray with a simple notion: “it’s either me or them” and never question why the cultist hordes require the culling until the game ends.

[b]Strafe like a cheetah kick like a mule[/b]
One of the major factors contributing to the retro feel of the game is Duskdude’s insane movement capabilities. Not only the player can scale ridiculously steep surfaces, strafe jumping continuously increases movement speed allowing the protagonist to traverse more open levels of the game in a matter of seconds. However, extraordinary agility would mean little without an arsenal to back it up with. 

Tools of the trade come in an impressive variety of 10 weapons to choose from. Pleasantly, all of them sound and feel exactly as powerful as they should be. Furthermore, short of humble pistol and perhaps sickles, all weapons are perfectly viable throughout the entire game. Let’s take a closer look, shotguns come in 2 flavours – double barrel and lever-action, the latter having an akimbo option for considerable punch and looking smooth. Followed by a machinegun, being basically a better pistol, a hunting rifle – trading fire rate for ability to one-shot an enemy across half the map. Next up is crossbow, firing magical bolts capable of piercing walls as well as enemies, a mortar allowing the player to manually detonate grenades for greater control, and finally a riveter – essentially a rapidly firing rocket launcher. As icing on the cake, this line-up includes a magical sword taking on new properties based on the player’s current health. Curiously, every weapon can be acquired during the first episode out of three, provided you find them in the secrets. However, all of these shiny murder-toys would mean little without a worthy array of monsters to point them at.
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2792091939 [/url]
[b]Touch from the beyond[/b]
DUSK provides a considerable variety of meat for the grinder, introducing fresh types of enemies at a steady pace. While the opponents are designed to visually fit the episode of their origin, they all share a characteristic of being ostentatiously evil. Even the more mundane cultists and soldiers, have their faces obscured to strip a faintest notion of humanity. Less evident but equally important is how long-range enemies have a distinct visual clue, allowing the player to easily recognise priority targets over large areas – such as flashing green light on the side of otherwise grey turret. An important facet of the game’s enemies is that DUSK has no hitscanners – every ranged enemy in the game fires a projectile that can be dodged or blocked, however their speed varies greatly between difficulty levels. For a truly retro, punishing experience Cero Miedo is highly recommended, as frankly DUSK isn’t particularly challenging for a significant part of its runtime.

On the danger note, the definite cherry on top of the mound of corpses is DUSK’s oppressive atmosphere. It’s quite unique how this title manages to be legitimately eerie at times, despite the player being in control of an unstoppable murder machine. Yes, you may have just shot 40 cultists but somehow monstrous wheezing down your neck on a dark staircase still gets under your skin. There are multiple aspects coming together to earn DUSK its “Horror” tag. Perhaps chief among them would be the soundtrack by Andrew Hulshult, full of both creepy ambient and heavy riffs ready to boot during the thickest of fights.
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2792093111[/url]
Another key component would be the level design itself. Each one of the three episodes has a distinct visual theme to it. Level scale and visual quality are also steadily increasing. Admittedly DUSK starts slow in that regard, with first episode of the foothills starring relatively mundane mix of run-down rural areas and mines. However, already at this early stage, this title hints that it is fully aware of the player’s expectations and aims to sweep the rug from under their feet whenever possible. As soon as, the second episode begins, the game starts to gradually unveil its hand, introducing a myriad of memorable set pieces. Episode two has an industrial aesthetic which becomes increasingly infernal, while the final chapter is both gothic and otherworldly. Despite its chunky looks, DUSK proves that low-poly truly can be an artstyle with its legitimately impressive visuals.

[b]Rats in the walls[/b]
Last but not least noteworthy aspect of the game is DUSK’s many secrets. In a truly retro fashion even the smallest level contains several of them, stashed away behind off-coloured wall or a hidden switch. Some secrets may appear a little crazy at first, however there is an inherent logic behind them and once you find a couple, treasure hunting suddenly becomes easier and more fun. Take note that on higher difficulty levels secrets are a must, as they don’t include extras but crucial means of survival. 

When it comes to issues with this title, I would legitimately struggle to find any at all. I have noticed but a single minor bug throughout my replays - how enemies occasionally struggle to spot the player going up the stairs, idly exposing themselves to damage. Furthermore, the deathmatch multiplayer mode of Duskworld is dead as a doornail. Its existence is a nice touch however, do bring your friends if you wish to try it out.

All things considered, DUSK truly is a prime example of its chosen genre. If you are a PC gaming veteran hailing from a faraway land of the 90’s, DUSK is a nostalgia trip bound to tick all the right boxes. Should you happen to enjoy shooters in general, this title is a [i]modern classic[/i] worthy of the moniker. Beating DUSK feels like completing a crazy fun fair ride – the moment it ended and the rush faded away, I felt compelled to yell “again” and hop right back into it.

[h1]The return to form for first person shooters[/h1]

[b]THIS.[/b]

This is the game I have been waiting for. DOOM 2016 may have started the comeback to the style of 1990's FPS, but it was Dusk that cemented the return.  When I first saw this game in 2017, I was truly hyped, which is something that rarely happens with me and videogames nowadays.  

David Szymanski has a passion for the FPS of old and it shows in this game. The first thing many people notice is the visuals, which is not just a choice for nostalgia's sake, but also an aesthetic choice as it adds to the atmosphere and mood of the game.  Like a certain id founder implied, gameplay is what makes an FPS, and Dusk delivers and then some.  Your arsenal of 10 weapons is excellently crafted, from the sickles, which can reflect enemy projectiles, to the Super Shotgun that calls back to DOOM II's legendary musket, to the Riveter, which can reduce entire rooms of monsters to piles of gibs with its high fire rate of explody mayhem.  

The player can reach high movement speed with strafe jumping, which is made easier to execute than Quake's method.  The player can dance circles around enemies and lay them to waste without taking a scratch.  No enemy in Dusk uses hitscan attacks, which I think is a good decision as the ability to dodge the enemy's offense is entirely dependent on the player.  

Speaking of enemies, the bestiary contains challenging and memorable enemies that help make this a true classic.  The ones that I will remember the most are the Wendigo, the tanky and hard-hitting Cart Dog, and the nightmare-inducing Horror.  Although enemy AI is straight out of the 90's, they are encountered in groups and situations that test the player's ability.

In classic id Software fashion, Dusk features powerups that can turn overwhelming odds into your favor.  The Fast Fire Totem is self-explanatory, but you can pick up more than one to turn your akimbo shotguns into a full-auto room clearer and your Riveter into a boss deleter.   The Climbing Hooks (actually called "Climbing Thing" in-game) allow you to scale walls and leap great distances Spider-Man style, which can lead you to some imaginative secret areas.  The Serum of Blistering Heat temporarily turns the gameplay into SuperHot, with time moving extremely slowly while the player stands still and time moving normally during player movement, which can allow the player ample time to assess enemy placement and attacks.  It also allows one to easily see the impressive explosion and gibbing effects.  Try to combine this with the Fast Fire Totem for a better Neo feel.

[h1]A Masterclass in FPS level design[/h1]

To me, the three biggest highlights of Dusk are the level design, the audio design, and the soundtrack.  David has put in his research in FPS level design. Each episode's levels are themed, with Episode 1 being inspired by Blood and Redneck Rampage, Episode 2 with S.T.A.L.K.E.R. themes, and Episode 3 has an imaginative Lovecraftian and otherworldly feel.  Some standouts include: the Episode 1 level Old Time Religion, which has a setting sun that bathes the majority of the level in a beautiful orange-purple light and a hauntingly serene song that fits perfectly with the setting; the Episode 2 level The Escher Labs, which is a creative blend of the Black Mesa areas of Half-Life and the surreal architecture of Constantine's Mansion of Thief: The Dark Project; and the Episode 3 level Homecoming, in which the entire map is literally flipped while playing it.  

 [h1]A musical genius[/h1]

To me, a videogame is made even more fun and engaging when it has the sound and music that enrich the gameplay.   Dusk's audio is handled by the awesomely talented Andrew Hulshult, whose previous work includes the soundtrack to the 2013 remake of Rise of the Triad.  I first heard of him from a series of remakes/remixes of songs from DOOM (1993).  They are some of the best crafted remixes of classic DOOM music I have  heard.  

When I heard that he was signed up to do the soundtrack of Dusk, it only added to the hype as I love his DOOM remixes and I could hardly wait to hear what he would compose for Dusk.  His soundtrack really hit me when I reached E1M3, Old Time Religion. The song, called "Ashes to Ashes, Dusk to Dusk," is a hauntingly serene piece that conjures feelings of nostalgia and calmness.  Andrew's songs for Dusk include industrial metal songs such as "Alienation Akimbo," "Keepers of the Gate," "Occultivated," and especially "Departure to Destruction" that provide the adrenaline rush that goes so well combat. In addition, there are plenty of ambient tracks that evoke various emotions.  Such emotional songs that I enjoy most are "A View From Below," "Ashes to Ashes, Dusk to Dusk," "Green Skies," "Beautiful Blasphemy," and "This is Your Life."  Andrew's work with Dusk's music has resulted in a truly memorable aural experience and one of my all-time favorite videogame soundtracks.  

The work Andrew has done since Dusk has cemented him as not only one of my favorite videogame composers, but one of my all-time favorite musicians.  He has since composed for games such as Amid Evil, Wrath: Aeon of Ruin, Prodeus, and Nightmare Reaper.  He even got to work on an official id Software game with Quake Champions, with one song from it, "Goroth," being featured in DOOM Eternal as an unlockable song.  

It was satisfying as a fan than when he was named one of the composers for DOOM Eternal's 2 DLC expansions.  Along with David Levy and most likely on short notice due to Mick Gordon's departure, they were able to churn out some remarkable songs for The Ancient Gods and expose their music to more people.  Seeing Andrew go from a fan of id Software who made some powerful remixes of classic DOOM music to the unofficial composer of the retro FPS revival to official composer of DOOM has been a journey that I, as well as many other fans in the community, are happy to have witnessed and is immensely satisfying.  

Andrew and David are responsible for the game's sound effects.  The sound of the weapons are powerful and meaty. Each enemy can be identified just from the sounds it makes while moving or idling.  Voice acting is provided by Andrew Hulshult, New Blood CEO Dave Oshry, David Szymanski, Natalya Ivanova, and an appearance from a legendary figure in videogame voice acting. I won't spoil who they are, but their talents live again in New Blood's releases.  One would think that the sound of "HUP" over and over again while strafe jumping would grate on their nerves, but David has, seemingly by some miracle, made this sound tolerable.  

The negatives that Dusk has are very few and are nitpicky at most.  The only cons about Dusk I can find are small bugs that are rare to occur and do not take away from the overall experience.  A co-op mode would have been good to have, but it's not essential to the game.  

[h1]A WORTHY revivial[/h1][b](tl;dr: BUY THIS GAME!)[/b]

Dusk is not just a call-back to retro FPS, but it manages to stand with the all-time classics as a peer.  I am definitely looking forward to David Szymanski's future works. Dusk is truly an unforgettable experience that I will keep revisiting.  The triumph of Dusk has led to the revival of first-person shooters made in the classic 90's style, with numerous developers creating their own throwback shooters, or "boomer shooters," with a focus on gameplay, complex levels, and fast action.  Special mention goes to Dave Oshry, Producer of Dusk and CEO of New Blood Interactive, who has to be the most down-to-earth and meme-tastic CEO of a videogame publisher today.  He enjoys interacting with the fans on Twitter, answering technical issues, clarifying the background of the protagonist of Dusk (Duskdude or The Intruder), and providing free Steam keys to fans short on money or just when he feels like it.  If only CEO's of AAA game companies were more like him...

Thanks for reading and keep on hanging in there.

One hell of a boomer shooter.

Story:

DUSK is very light on plot as it's main focus is gameplay, but there is somewhat of a plot going on in the game. You play as Dusk Dude. Through his travels he comes across a rural town of Dusk and the place is overrun with weird cultists and military fighting each other while you're caught in their crossfire and as you plunge deeper into the town you find that there's something otherworldly waiting to be unleashed.

Dusk is one of those games where you have to piece the story together yourself. However I feel like the visuals and the way the story advances is so interesting it actually helps the player to really get into the bizarre world of Dusk better. Honestly some of the moments in Episode 3 especially were just simply amazing.

Graphics:

DUSK goes for that boomer shooter aesthetic (think Quake) and honestly it nails it perfectly. I loved everything about it's visual design, from the crazy environments to the great enemy designs. There's a great range of enemies from normal looking military grunts and cult members and then once the creatures get unleashed then you get even more crazy and creepy looking enemies.

The environments are also really great and honestly I really loved how varied these environments are. From farms to caves and military camps and others I don't want to name. Also the game manages to mix colors so well that I honestly was in awe, one moment you can be exploring a very mute looking farmhouse and then soon you can be exploring a pretty colorful looking temple, DUSK knows when to use colors to it's advantage and it works really well. 

Audio:

First of all I have to give props to Andrew Hulshult for the soundtrack which kicks so much ass. There's plenty of absolutely great tracks that match the hectic tone of the fights and then there's tracks that match the creepy tone it goes for, it's just so well made that I can't really give enough praise. 

Other sound effects like guns sounds incredibly meaty and I could never get sick of the super shotgun blowing enemies into chunks, it was just music to my ears. Every gun sounds like it packs quite the punch and honestly after so many disappointments I'm glad this one nails it perfectly. 

Gameplay:

DUSK is again very similar to the shooters of the 90's and by that I mean you will kill everything that moves and look around the environment to find keys so you can advance further. I have to say that DUSK plays like an absolute dream. Everything from the movement, to the shooting just mixes so well that I loved every single minute playing it. 

The levels are designed in a way so you can strafe jump around fast enough around the enemy attacks and gun them down with quick aiming it's so satisfying, especially when you enter an arena where there's an army of enemies and you slaughter them all like a total badass. 

The game is split across three episodes and honestly each progressing episode gets better as it goes along. Episode 3 was especially amazing, because the scale of the fights and set pieces are unlike anything in the previous two episodes and it serves as the perfect culmination to the story.  

However there is one minor nitpick of mine and that's the level design of Episode 2. I do think the episode is better than the first one overall, I can't say that I'm entirely huge on the level design. Quite a few of the levels felt a bit too cramped and got me killed a few times when I had simply no place to go to avoid enemies.

Verdict:

DUSK kicks ass, plain and simple. It's such a fun throwback shooter that I cannot recommend enough. It has tons of heart and it shows, from the fast paced and frenetic gameplay to the great soundtrack it just blends together so well I could not stop playing, not to mention the extra modes after you're done with the story make the price worth it. So just stop reading this and go get DUSK. 

Final Rating:
9.5/10

Pros:
+ Incredibly fun gameplay
+ Awesome soundtrack
+ Visuals are great
+ Tons of content 
+ Audio design is spectacular

Cons:
- Level design is pretty weak in Episode 2
